Hi, dumbtickles here. I am going to be helping out Cris, a former Uber Driver with this AMA.

Cris is in his late 30s and lives in California with his family. He drove Uber in two major Uber markets including San Francisco.

He did it for a while until he decided that it was no longer to his benefit to drive for the company. He has since moved on and has no plans to drive for Uber any longer.
I drove for UBER for a few months to make ends meet. AMA.
Ever get any weirdos? Creepy/dangerous encounters etc?
No. Most people were normal. Had one gay guy talking about all the guys he's nailed since moving to the city and how he contracted an std. That might of been the weirdest.

Let's get these out of the way

How much money did he make? How much did he work? How much up/down time was there during work?

Can you tell us any more about the decision that it was no longer a benefit? Why would he not drive for Uber any more?

At its peak I was making around $400/week working 30-40 hours per week. In my home town I could go an hour or two in between rides. In San Francisco, about 15 minutes. It wasn't a benefit and I wouldn't drive for them again because uber made it impossible to make money after a while. There's a lot of talk about surge pricing but more often then not uber is dropping their prices. In the short 4 months I drove for them they had 3 price drops. Eventually I was working more hours and making less. Also if you have issues with a passenger uber is NOT on your side as a driver.
Is that kind of money after paying your expenses? Do you think someone would have more success working near an airport or late weekends around nightlife?

That does not include expenses. Airports are pretty tightly regulated. You need to be informed about the one near you or you can face pretty steep fines. Working weekends and late nights is a way to increase your chances of getting rides. Concerts and big events are another. Depends where you live. If you're in SF or LA or NY all you have to do is get in your car and turn on your phone. You'll get calls guaranteed. If you're in a smaller market you may need to get more creative.
Do you think Uber should be regulated like Taxis? Why or why not?
Drivers should have to go through more screening for the sake of the public. Beyond that I don't feel sorry for the taxis.

Do you think it's competitive as a driver?

If yes, would you think that to make a decent living as a driver you would need to find an area far enough from cities with many existing drivers, toward a rural area that somehow has high demand for uber rides? Do places like that exist?

The only way to be competitive is to drive for both uber and lyft. I didn't and wish I did. Both companies discourage it but who cares. You have an uber phone or app and a lyft phone or app. You pick up whichever goes off first. As far as the condition you mentioned. No it doesn't exist.

What are your thoughts on Uber making it a company policy to not want any of their drivers to have handguns in their own personal vehicles. Talking about states like Texas were everyone from the 21 yr old to the lil old granny has a gun for protection. For background, here is the incident that had Uber change their policy. "Back in April, an Uber driver stopped a possible mass murder. He saw the alleged suspect open fire on a group of people in Chicago. The Uber driver was legally carrying his hand gun and stopped the attacker."

Not trying to get into politics about guns and stuff, just wanna know what a recent driver thinks about that.

Easy to Search Database of Incentives for Energy Efficiency and Renewables

Working on projects across the US adds quite a bit of variety in the availability of building incentives. Building incentives are essentially free money (or something else of value to the building owner) for doing X, Y, or Z as described by the incentives program - an example of this might be installing high efficiency lighting to get a direct payment or tax credit. This site makes it trivial to find incentives across the US, and for green building practitioners, this opens up an opportunity to help convince building owners or developers to include green building strategies at a reduced cost to the owner.

This was my secret weapon when I worked on several US projects as a green building consultant a few years back (the projects regularly included scope to investigate incentives availability). Use it on your next project to see if there are any incentive related opportunities you might not have considered.
